summary: Expanded Related Work to cover evidence reranking, compact graph retrieval, and complementary drug-repositioning approaches, and clarified the contribution (manuscript pp. 3–4).
Added learned and automatically selected coefficients, equal-weight controls, and cross-dataset transfer (manuscript Section 4.5, p. 14; Supplementary Section S12, pp. 18–23).
Added matched-budget subgraph comparisons and quantitative retention analyses (manuscript Section 4.6, p. 15; Supplementary Section S13, pp. 23–28).
Clarified the fixed-candidate evaluation scope and updated numerical reporting, as detailed in our response to Comment 4 (manuscript Section 4.2, pp. 11–12; Table 3, p. 13).
Documented repoDB preprocessing, entity alignment, and leakage control (manuscript Section 4.1, pp. 10–11; Supplementary Section S11.1, pp. 17–18).
Refined the discussion of multi-source fusion, the limitations, and the conclusions (manuscript Section 5, pp. 17–18; Section 6, pp. 18–19).

1: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need for clearer positioning. Related Work now discusses RankRAG, G-Retriever, GRAG, and SubgraphRAG, explaining their approaches to context ranking, compact graph retrieval, and learned triple selection (manuscript pp. 3–4, particularly Section 2.3, p. 4).

We have also revised the novelty claims to emphasize the integration of biomedical evidence cues for candidate reranking and graph selection. This scope is stated in the Abstract (p. 1), the Introduction contributions (p. 3), the Discussion (pp. 17–18), and the Conclusion (pp. 18–19).
2: We thank the reviewer for this concern. We added validation-based coefficient search, a learned scorer using five shared features, and leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) transfer that excludes target calibration labels. Equal-weight controls isolate the effect of learning. For fuzzy retrieval, automatic selection compares 12 coefficient vectors at fixed candidate order and graph budget.

Learned weights improve candidate MRR over the original formula on four datasets and match it on PrimeKG; LODO gives higher point estimates on all five. Against equal weights, the exploratory 95% interval for the learned gain excludes zero only on repoDB. These findings support coefficient reuse within the evaluated benchmarks, with dataset-dependent benefits.

The main findings appear in manuscript Section 4.5 (p. 14) and Table 4 (p. 15). Supplementary Section S12 (pp. 18–23), including Tables S16–S24 (pp. 19–23), provides the fitting, transfer, ablation, and sensitivity analyses.
3: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Across all five datasets, we compared fuzzy retrieval with random sampling, coverage-based, score-based, breadth-first, PageRank, shortest-path, and relation-stratified selectors, fixing candidate order and the unique-edge budget. The analyses measure candidate coverage, reachability, labeled paths, and encoder representations across multiple budgets.

Fuzzy retrieval preserves incident evidence for all source-covered candidates, while three-hop reachability retention ranges from 0.4835 on Hetionet to 0.9546 on repoDB. It exceeds random selection on PharmKG, DRKG, and repoDB. Shortest-path selection retains more connectivity but covers fewer candidates on some datasets, demonstrating the distinction between candidate coverage and path preservation.
Manuscript Section 4.6 and Table 5 (p. 15) summarize these findings. Supplementary Section S13 (pp. 23–28), Tables S25–S29 (pp. 25–26), and Figs. S4–S6 (pp. 27–28) provide the detailed comparisons.
4: We thank the reviewer for drawing attention to the evaluation scope. SoftFuse-KGC targets candidate ordering and evidence selection within the backbone’s fixed top-20 set. On PrimeKG, candidate MRR@20 increases from 0.0646 to 0.1253 at unchanged Gold@20 of 0.240, while fuzzy retrieval reduces the graph from 59.93 to 32.34 triples. These results support ranking and evidence-efficiency gains at fixed candidate coverage. We clarify this scope in manuscript Section 4.2 (pp. 11–12), with results in Table 3 (p. 13).

During revision, we corrected FP16 overflow affecting 9/500 PrimeKG full-graph test cases and standardized E2E scoring. Re-evaluation used FP32 graph encoding and BF16 inference with unchanged checkpoints and splits and no excluded cases; for example, the source E2E MRR changed from 0.0476 to 0.0477 (manuscript Table 3, p. 13).

We also recalculated validation candidate MRR from candidate identifiers, assigning zero reciprocal rank to absent gold entities. The corrected values appear in manuscript Fig. 2 (p. 8) and Supplementary Section S1.1 (pp. 3–4), Table S6 (p. 11), and Table S13 (p. 15).
5: We thank the reviewer for identifying this missing detail. We retain repoDB diseases as local UMLS nodes and join DRKG molecular evidence through exact DrugBank compound identifiers, preserving gene identifiers and relations. No disease crosswalk or disease-to-gene conversion is applied. In the prepared DRKG map, 1,130 of 1,571 compounds match; unmatched compounds remain in the task.

Manuscript Section 4.1 (pp. 10–11, repoDB paragraph on p. 11) now describes this alignment. Supplementary Section S11.1 (pp. 17–18) details normalization, deduplication, label conflicts, graph construction, and splitting with held-out target triples excluded. Table S15 (p. 17) distinguishes local graph-ID coverage from cross-resource alignment.
6: We thank the reviewer for highlighting these relevant studies. Related Work discusses spatial–spectral fusion and FD-MSGL in Section 2.1 (manuscript pp. 3–4); both are included as References 45–46 (p. 23).

The final paragraph of the Discussion (Section 5, p. 18) explains how jointly learning molecular, interaction, and pathway representations with fusion weights could enrich candidate scoring and guide graph selection under edge-budget and path-retention objectives.
